title: Test-code complexity: its own population, its own series, or refused

dims.name: The verdict
dims.question: What happens to the complexity of this repo's test code?
dims.problem: This repo counts cyclomatic complexity for eight populations of product code. Every `*.test.ts` file is dropped before the count. More than half of this repo's functions therefore never reach the trend layer. This row decides what to do about that: build an instrument, refuse one, or wait. A careless pick either adds a panel nobody acts on, or leaves the enforcement code unmeasured forever.

opts.label: Refuse. Test code gets no complexity series.
Give test code its own population and its own series.
Fold test code into the eight existing populations.
Measure once by hand. Record the numbers. Build nothing.
Decide later, after the first product cap arms.

dims.name: The population boundary
dims.question: Which test files count as one population?
dims.problem: A population is the set of files one number describes. The product series use eight populations, one per declared scope. Test code offers three candidate boundaries: the gates alone, every test file as one set, or one test set per product scope. The boundary decides what a movement in the number can mean. A boundary that mixes unlike code produces a number nobody can attribute.

opts.label: No population. Nothing is grouped.
`gates/` alone. The constitution's enforcement code.
Every `*.test.ts` file, as one population.
One test population beside each declared scope.
No fixed boundary. Somebody picks the files when they ask.

dims.name: How a test population enters the counter
dims.question: What edit makes the counter see a test file?
dims.problem: `populationOf` in `scripts/lib/complexity.ts` reads one thing: a `scopes[].glob` from `stryker.scopes.json`, minus `*.test.ts`. The walk that feeds it drops test files too. `stryker.config.mjs` derives Stryker's mutation targets from the same `scopes[]` array. So the declaration file serves two instruments at once. This row decides which edit declares a test population, and each option pays a different price somewhere else.

opts.label: No declaration. `populationOf` stays as it is.
A new `scopes[]` entry in `stryker.scopes.json`.
A second list, beside `scopes[]`, read only by the counter.
Drop the `*.test.ts` filter from the population rule.
Run the counter by hand on a file list, when somebody asks.

dims.name: Which counts a test population emits
dims.question: Which of the four counts would a test series carry?
dims.problem: The trend layer emits four counts per population: `complexity-functions`, `complexity-mass`, `complexity-max` and `complexity-mass-over-10`. The first two grow with the codebase. The last two describe the worst functions, and only those two carry caps. This row decides which counts a test population would report. A count that cannot move is a panel with a flat line on it.

opts.label: None. No count is emitted for test code.
All four counts, as the product populations carry them.
`complexity-functions` and `complexity-mass` only.
`complexity-max` and `complexity-mass-over-10` only.
A fifth count, written for test code.

dims.name: Teeth
dims.question: Does a test series get a cap that refuses a deploy?
dims.problem: A cap is this repo's only teeth for a metric. It arms at the highest value seen across a twenty-run window. After that it moves down only, by hand. An armed cap makes `pnpm deploy:site` refuse when a scope exceeds it. The spec already refuses a per-function ceiling on a pull request, because *refactor this function* is not a finite diff. This row asks whether test code earns the surviving surface.

opts.label: No cap, because no series exists.
Cap it, as the product populations are capped.
A series with no cap. Report only.
Cap `complexity-max` alone. Leave the rest uncapped.
A per-function ceiling, red on a pull request.

dims.name: Reader and action
dims.question: Who reads the number, and what do they then do?
dims.problem: `gate-or-trend.md` §2 obliges a trend to name a reader and a cadence. A series that reaches nobody is deleted in effect, whatever the dashboard shows. This row names the person and the action. The ticket asks the same question in its own words: if there is no named action, that argues for refusal rather than for a quieter panel.

opts.label: Nobody, because no number exists.
The maintainer, at `pnpm deploy:site`, as today.
A dashboard panel. No reader is named.
A named review step before anyone edits a gate.

dims.name: Where the verdict is written down
dims.question: Which document carries the refusal?
dims.problem: A refusal that lives only in a closed ticket is invisible to the next session. This repo keeps three homes for such a record: the map's own spec, `docs/gates.md` under *Not gated, deliberately*, and `docs/adr/`. Each home carries a different promise about who reads it. The wrong home makes the next session re-derive the same numbers.

opts.label: The map's spec, `docs/spec/static-analysis-and-style.md`.
`docs/gates.md`, under *Not gated, deliberately*.
Its own record under `docs/adr/`.
Nowhere. Close the ticket and move on.

verdict-refuse.why: Test code gets no complexity population and no series. The measurement in this ticket is the whole deliverable.
rel: A refusal edits no code, so the population rule stays as it is.
The map's Destination asks for a verdict per candidate, in the spec.
notes: Refusal is a first-class result on this map. The Destination says so.
This option costs nothing to reverse. The counter already takes an explicit file list.

verdict-series.why: Test code gets its own populations and its own trend panels, beside the product ones.
rel: A series needs a declaration, and the current rule reads only product globs.
A trend must name a reader and a cadence.
A series that emits no count is not a series.

verdict-fold.why: Test files join the eight product populations. One number covers both kinds of code.
rel: Only the removal of the `*.test.ts` filter folds the two sets together.
A fold declares no new population. It widens the eight that exist.
notes: The ticket calls this almost certainly wrong. It moves every number at once and restarts every cap window.
Measured cost: mean complexity across all test functions is 1.37, against 2.92 for product code. A fold halves every mean.

verdict-once.why: Somebody measures test complexity by hand, records the numbers, and builds no instrument.
rel: A one-off measurement needs no declaration and no edit.
A one-off measurement emits no series.
notes: Nothing in this box rules this out, and this session did exactly this.
It differs from the chosen option in one way only: it makes no promise about the future.

verdict-later.why: The question waits until the first product cap arms and the repo learns what a cap costs.
rel: A deferral records no verdict, so it needs no home.
notes: The first cap arms after a twenty-run window fills. Nothing states when that happens.
A deferral with no date is a refusal that nobody has to defend.

boundary-none.why: No test files are grouped into anything. The eight product populations stay as they are.

boundary-hand.why: No boundary is fixed in advance. Somebody names the files each time a question arises.
rel: A boundary chosen per question cannot be declared in advance.
notes: A boundary that changes per question produces no series, because a series needs a stable denominator.
Nothing in this box rules this out. It is the configuration this session ran.

boundary-gates.why: The 38 gate specs become one population. The ticket's case: nothing tests the tests.
rel: `stryker.config.mjs` derives `mutate` from `scopes[]`, so Stryker then mutates gates/ and the dry run dies.
Gate test code peaks at complexity 9, so `complexity-max` is flat and `complexity-mass-over-10` is 0.
A cap arms at the highest observed value, and no gate test function passes 9.
notes: Measured: gate test code is indistinguishable from package test code. Mean 1.42 against 1.41, max 9 against 10.
A `gates/**/*.ts` entry measures the four helper files, not the 38 gates. That is 24 functions with a maximum of 6.

boundary-all.why: Every test file in the repo forms one population, across packages, scripts and gates.
rel: Across all 1931 test functions the maximum is 10, so `complexity-mass-over-10` is identically 0.
A cap on a count that is always 0 can never go red.
A `scopes[]` glob cannot reach a test file, because two filters drop it first.
notes: One population across three roots hides which root moved. That is the attribution cost.
Measured: 79.5% of test functions score 1. The product figure is 48.6%.

boundary-twin.why: Each declared scope gains a test twin, so a panel pair sits under each product panel.
rel: Every twin has a maximum of 10 or less and a mass-over-10 of 0.
A `scopes[]` glob cannot reach a test file, because two filters drop it first.
Eight more populations need eight more declarations, and `scopes[]` cannot hold them.
notes: This boundary doubles the panel count from 32 to 64, for counts that do not move.
It also leaves gates/ out, because gates/ matches no product scope. That is the ticket's own question 2.

mech-none.why: Nothing changes. `populationOf` reads a product glob and drops every test file.
rel: A fold needs the `*.test.ts` filter removed, and this option keeps it.
A ceiling needs a per-function count over test files, and no declaration produces one.

mech-hand.why: Nothing is declared. Somebody calls the counter with an explicit file list when a question arises.
rel: A hand run emits nothing to the trend layer.
notes: `complexityOf` already takes an explicit file list, so this option needs no code at all.
This session used exactly this route to produce every number in the resolution.

mech-scope.why: A test population is declared the way the spec says a new population enters: a `scopes[]` entry.
rel: Two filters drop every test file, so this entry produces no test count at all.
#239 run: gates/**/*.ts yields 4 helper files, 24 functions
notes: The spec names this as the only way gates/ enters. It does not say the entry also declares a mutation scope.
G38 (`mutation-scope`) refuses a deploy when a declared scope produces no mutant. This entry produces the opposite problem: a dry run that dies.

mech-second-list.why: A list beside `scopes[]` declares test populations, and only the complexity counter reads it.
rel: A second declaration list is a hard-to-reverse decision, so it owes a record.
notes: The spec refuses this in one line: *No second list: G38 already holds that file to the tree.*
A second list is unheld. Nothing compares it to the tree, so a renamed directory drops a population in silence.

mech-drop-filter.why: The `*.test.ts` filter leaves `populationOf`, so every declared glob picks up its test files.
rel: The filter is repo-wide, so its removal folds test code into the product populations instead.
Every product number moves at once, so every armed cap must disarm and every window restarts.
notes: The walk drops test files a second time, in `isSourceFile`. Both filters must go.
Measured effect on one scope: `packages/core/src` moves from 84 functions to 283, and its mean falls from 3.68 to 1.95.

series-none.why: Nothing is emitted. The four families keep their eight populations of product code.
rel: A panel needs a number, and no count is emitted for test code.

series-four.why: A test population reports the same four counts a product population reports.
rel: The four counts arrive with the cap rule the spec attaches to two of them.
Four more families need the reader that the existing four name.
notes: Two of the four are measured flat on every candidate boundary. This option ships two dead panels per population.

series-uncapped.why: Only the two counts that grow with the codebase are emitted. Neither carries a cap.
rel: The spec leaves `complexity-functions` and `complexity-mass` uncapped, because they grow legitimately.
A count of functions names no function, so no reviewer can act on it.
notes: You raise both counts when you add a test. That is Clause B's shape, applied to a series rather than to a gate.
The number that results is a measure of test volume. `pnpm test` already reports that faster.

series-capped.why: Only the two worst-case counts are emitted, so a panel shows the worst test function per population.
rel: A worst-case count is actionable only if somebody reads the named function.
notes: Measured dead on arrival: `complexity-mass-over-10` is 0 for every candidate test population in this repo.
`complexity-max` sits at 10 for all test files, 9 for gates/ and 8 for scripts/. Three populations, three flat lines.

series-new.why: A fifth count is designed for test code, for example the count of helpers above complexity 5.
rel: A fifth measure changes what the trend layer means, so it owes a record.
A new count needs a population to count over.
notes: Measured target size: 41 test functions score between 5 and 10. Two of them reach 10.
G36 (`trend-layer`) holds trend names to the rows in `docs/gates.md`, so a fifth family needs a fifth row.

cap-none.why: No cap exists, because there is no series for a cap to watch.

cap-ceiling.why: A per-function complexity ceiling goes red on a pull request when any test function passes it.
rel: A ceiling reads a per-function number, which only the worst-case counts carry.
notes: The spec already refuses this shape for product code, in §4, on Clause A: *refactor this function* is not a finite diff.
It also refuses a pre-commit hook that blocks, because `--no-verify` makes it a gate anyone can skip.

cap-capped.why: A test population's cap arms after its window fills, and `pnpm deploy:site` then refuses a breach.
rel: A cap refuses at the deploy, which is where the maintainer meets it.
A cap needs a series, and a refusal builds none.
notes: A cap armed at 10 refuses the first test helper that reaches 11. The remedy is *refactor this test helper*.
The spec already calls that remedy insufficient for Clause A, in its refusal of a per-function ceiling.

cap-uncapped.why: The series reports and never refuses. Only its own silence is red.
rel: A trend with no teeth still owes a named reader and a cadence.

cap-max-only.why: `complexity-max` carries a cap. The other counts report only.
rel: `complexity-max` is not in the uncapped pair, so this option needs it emitted.
A cap on a count pinned at 10 arms at 10 and never moves.

reader-none.why: Nobody reads a test complexity number, because none is produced.

reader-deploy.why: The maintainer meets the number at `pnpm deploy:site`, beside the mutation scores and the four product families.
rel: A named reader needs a document that tells the next session who reads what.
notes: `pnpm deploy:site` already prints the trend record first and refuses a stale one, per G39.

reader-panel.why: The number appears on the Grafana dashboard. No document names a reader or an action.
rel: A panel with no named reader needs no record either.
notes: The spec forbids this shape: a trend must name a reader and a cadence.
An unread dashboard and a deleted one are the same artifact. The spec says so in those words.

reader-review.why: Before anyone edits a gate, they read the list of test helpers above a stated complexity.
rel: A gate-edit review reads gate code, so it needs the gates as a population.
notes: This is the one live action the measurement suggests. The complexity in test code sits in named helpers.
Measured: `shelfCost` at 10, `citations`, `indexHtml` and `coreImports` at 7. All are helpers, not test bodies.
A review step is a process, not a series. It needs no trend layer at all.

record-spec.why: The verdict lands in the spec this map produces, beside the other candidates' verdicts.
rel: The spec records a verdict per candidate, and *later* is not a verdict.

record-gates-md.why: The refusal joins the eight entries under *Not gated, deliberately*.
notes: That section records rules no gate protects. A refused series is not a rule, so the fit is poor.
#229 chose this home for a style-rule refusal. A style rule is a candidate gate; this candidate is a trend.

record-adr.why: The verdict gets its own file under `docs/adr/`, with the reasoning carried verbatim.
notes: AGENTS.md asks for a record when a decision is hard to reverse, surprising, and a real trade-off.
This refusal is cheap to reverse, so it fails the first of the three tests.

record-nowhere.why: The closed ticket carries the answer. No document changes.
notes: The map's Decisions-so-far still points at the ticket, so the answer is not lost.
It is lost to anyone who reads the spec instead of the map, which is the audience the Destination names.

suspected: series-uncapped conflicts with verdict-series, because Clause B rules out a check you turn green by adding tests. Clause B is written for gates, and a trend is not a gate, so this is an analogy rather than a rule.
boundary-gates requires its own series, because gate code is the code most likely to be subtly wrong. Nothing measured supports the claim that complexity finds that wrongness.

presets.title: As recommended
presets.text: The chosen set: refuse the series, record the verdict in the spec, keep the measurement. Open the two rows that carry the argument.

presets.title: The cheap route
presets.text: One population of every test file, the two volume counts, no cap. The cheapest instrument anybody would build. Read what it fails to require.

steps.label: One population of all test files

presets.title: Do the gates deserve a population
presets.text: The ticket's own case, selected. A `scopes[]` entry for gates/, with the worst-case counts. Both edges out of it are red.

presets.text: Measure once by hand, build nothing. Nothing in this box rules it out, and this session did exactly that.
